text: Applying to a PhD is a team sport that most students play alone.

Offer room gives one student a team, inside the chat app she already uses. Six AI agents, each starting from a different place: official pages, advisors' papers, her own record read cold, her story, money, and interview practice. They agree, add, or push back with evidence. She decides.
It's built with Switch. One template creates six Claude Code agents and five Discord rooms. The agents hand work to each other by mention, like teammates.
Meet two applicants. Both are fictional, and I type their side of the chat.
Priya, in Tamil Nadu, wants AI that understands her grandmother's Tamil. Her family set aside three hundred and fifty dollars: enough for two applications.
Maya, in El Paso, is the first in her family to go to college. She fixes speech recognition for people who switch between Spanish and English, and she has three hundred dollars saved.
Priya asks the team room: which two of Washington, Maryland and Cornell? Scout answers first, from the programs' own pages: Washington and Cornell, for cost and deadlines. Then it hands off.

Mentor disagrees, with papers: Maryland has the clearest lab for her work. Critic checks both against Priya's record and closes the round: where they agree, where they split, and what only she can decide.

Then she pushes back. Mentor runs a topic search, finds a Cornell professor it had missed, and says so first: I was wrong. Critic withdraws two of its own claims. The team now agrees on Washington and Cornell.
At the funding desk, one to one, the same question from both students.
For Maya, all three fees fit in her budget, and every school has a waiver she qualifies for, quoted line by line, with the date to ask.
For Priya, on a student visa, only Cornell's waiver is open. When a test-score page wouldn't load, the agent said so, and asked her.
In the interview room, the agent plays a real professor, built only from her public papers, and says it's practice. It scores each answer, and tells Priya to cut the line where she doubts herself.
Then it digs: points of what, and is it really code-switching? Priya owns the gap and names the experiment she'd run. Depth goes from three to five, and the next question digs again.
Every fact carries a source. A draft checker fails any sentence without one, and any paper no tool actually returned. And no agent sends, submits or pays. People do.
Getting in is the start, not the finish. Offer room. Built with Switch.
